name: Недостатньо матеріалу для мату
description:
The previous lesson was about simplifying into a pawn endgame. It is also possible to simplify into other types of endgames. In this lesson we will focus on defense. Usually when you are behind in material, it is better not to exchange pieces. An exception to this is if the attacker is left with a position in which they can no longer give mate with that extra material.

We will cover the following situations in this lesson:

King and knight against king (example 1)
King and bishop against king (example 2)
King and 'wrong' bishop + edge pawn against king (example 3)
King and two knights against king (example 4)
The aim of this lesson is to simplify into one of the above situations, so that you can still save a seemingly lost position with half a point (see examples 5 and 6).

What do you have to do?

Simplify into an endgame in which the other player has insufficient material to mate.

examples.text:
We know from mating with the queen or rook that we must drive the other player's king to the corner or edge. Unfortunately, this is not sufficient if a player only has a knight.

In the example, the king is in check, but not mate. The king can still move to the side.

No matter what you try, you will never succeed in mating with king and knight against king. Check this for yourself. Suppose the knight is on f6 instead of g6, then white has succeeded in taking all the squares from the king. However, the king is then not in check: it is stalemate!

Also for king and bishop against king, the same applies as with king and knight against king in Example 1. Mating is not possible. Here the king can move aside. With a bishop on e6 instead of f6 the black king cannot move, but is not in check. It is stalemate instead of mate.

There are even situations when having a bishop and a pawn are not sufficient to win. Above you can see that white has an edge pawn and a 'wrong' colored bishop. Wrong means that the color of the bishop does not match the color of the pawn's promotion square. Here white has a light-squared bishop and square h8 is black. If the defender can occupy the promotion square or the adjacent square with the king in time (in this case squares h8 and g8), then the position is a draw. Even if white would have several pawns on the h-line, they cannot win. The black king moves back and forth between the promotion square and the square next to it (or if the king moves the square in front of the promotion square; here h7).

So in the example, black plays 1...Kh8. If white then plays with the king, the black king moves forward and white cannot advance. If the bishop moves off the a2-g8 diagonal, the black king moves aside and if the bishop plays on the same diagonal then it is stalemate (unless white plays 2.Bg8, but then black simply captures the bishop).

It is also stalemate if white moves the pawn forward. By the way, notice here the important difference between a 'good' colored bishop. If the bishop from e6 would have been on e5, the black king cannot flee to the corner and white does promote.

Remarkably, even with a king and two knights against a king the position is a draw. Unlike examples 1 and 2, mate is possible, however it requires the defender to play very stupidly. See above. If black now plays 1...Kh8, white gives mate with 2.Nf7. However, if the defender is careful and does not voluntarily step into the corner, the other player will never succeed in mating. Check this out for yourself! So here black plays 1...Kf8.

Black threatens to promote. If black succeeds, white has a big problem. Fortunately, white can use a special attack to sacrifice the bishop for the pawn: 1.Bd3+ (double attack!) 1...Kb4 2.Bxe2 Nxe2. White has lost a bishop. Normally bad news, but since Black now only has a knight left, they cannot mate. Draw by insufficient material!

Black only has one pawn left and even gives it away: 1...h3!. If White does not react to this, Black captures the pawn and White has only a bishop left. They cannot mate with just a bishop. But if white captures the pawn, then white has an edge pawn with the wrong colored bishop. The black king walks to the corner (h8) and nothing can happen to him there.

Not good, by the way, is 1...Kg3. Black wants to make the next move 2...h3, but with 2.Bd7 white can prevent this. Black will eventually lose the pawn and with a bishop and a g-pawn white cannot win.
